summary: Container shipping is moving from record pandemic-era profits back to losses as freight rates fall below costs and new ship supply outpaces demand. Executives at Hapag-Lloyd, Maersk and CMA CGM are cutting costs and warning against price wars, while analysts expect a standoff over who cuts capacity first. Lower shipping costs help ease goods inflation, but rising canal fees, Panama Canal disruption and a $1 trillion decarbonization bill loom for carriers.
one_line: After record 2021-22 profits, container carriers face losses for the next few years as oversupply drives rates below costs, with rising costs ahead.
key_facts: The biggest container carriers posted net income totaling $364 billion in 2021 and 2022, per figures compiled by industry veteran John McCown, after a decade of scant profits.
Carriers will likely drift back into the red this quarter as rates fall below costs and are expected to stay there for the foreseeable future.
Shipping lines move 80% of the world's merchandise trade.
Hapag-Lloyd CEO Rolf Habben Jansen said, "I'm certainly concerned about the next 24 to 36 months" and expects a downturn.
Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Stephane Kovatchev said Maersk's free cash flow, $27 billion last year, may drop about 80% this year and could turn negative in 2024.
Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd and CMA CGM, all top-five players controlling about one-third of container capacity, said they are cutting costs, with some fearing the slump lasts at least through 2024.
CMA CGM CFO Ramon Fernandez warned that price wars hurt not only those who start them but everyone; past price wars contributed to consolidation and at least one major bankruptcy before the pandemic.
Container ships take two to three years to build and typically operate for about 25 years, making it hard to time capacity with the business cycle.
Short-term capacity tools include canceling voyages, suspending services, letting charters expire, idling ships or scrapping old ones.
Transiting the Suez Canal from Asia will be 15% costlier next year, per the canal authority, while the drought-stricken Panama Canal faces long waits, surcharges and detours.
The industry faces about $1 trillion in investment in the coming decades to decarbonize, and shipping enters the EU Emissions Trading System in January.
Flexport chief economist Phil Levy said inflationary pressure from goods has disappeared; Under Armour and Lovesac cited relief from lower ocean shipping expenses.
CMA CGM's Rodolphe Saade has diversified into an airline, ports, logistics and media; the Saade family is worth about $19 billion, down from $33 billion in April.
